battle.title: Handshake or Hurl
battle.description: TCP's careful promises against UDP's fire-and-forget speed.

questions.text: Which statement about UDP is correct?
options: It retransmits lost datagrams automatically
It delivers datagrams in the order they were sent
It is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery or order
It opens a connection with a three-way handshake
questions.answer: It is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery or order
questions.explanation: UDP just sends datagrams: no connection setup, no retransmission, no ordering. Those guarantees are exactly what TCP adds, at the cost of extra latency and overhead.

questions.text: What is the correct order of the TCP three-way handshake?
options: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
SYN, ACK, SYN-ACK
ACK, SYN, SYN-ACK
SYN-ACK, SYN, ACK
questions.explanation: The client sends SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK (acknowledging and sending its own SYN), and the client confirms with ACK. Only then is the connection established and data can flow.

questions.text: You are building a live video call where an occasional glitch is fine but delay is not. Which transport fits best?
options: TCP, because reliability matters most in real time
UDP, because a late retransmitted packet is useless
TCP with a larger window to hide latency
TCP, because UDP cannot carry video
questions.answer: UDP, because a late retransmitted packet is useless
questions.explanation: A retransmitted video frame arrives too late to be shown, and TCP's in-order delivery would stall newer frames behind a lost one (head-of-line blocking). UDP lets the app skip lost data and keep going.

questions.text: A TCP segment is lost in transit. What does TCP do?
options: Closes the connection and reports an error at once
Ignores it because the checksum already protects the data
Leaves the application to detect the gap and resend
Retransmits it after missing an ACK and slows its sending rate
questions.answer: Retransmits it after missing an ACK and slows its sending rate
questions.explanation: TCP notices the missing acknowledgement (timeout or duplicate ACKs), retransmits, and treats the loss as a congestion signal by shrinking its congestion window. The application never sees the gap.

questions.text: What is the TCP receive window (flow control) designed to prevent?
options: A fast sender overflowing the receiver's buffer
Routers on the path becoming congested
Packets being corrupted on the wire
Two apps using the same port number
questions.answer: A fast sender overflowing the receiver's buffer
questions.explanation: Flow control is about the receiver: it advertises how much buffer space is left. Router congestion is the job of congestion control, a separate mechanism that is the tempting wrong answer here.
